claims.claim: laya-train exists as a console script and as 'laya train'; builds items from CSV or JSONL, fine-tunes, fits calibration temperatures on a slice held out before training, saves a checkpoint that laya.load opens; runs on one device (CUDA, MPS or CPU).
claims.limits: Python package version 0.4.13 on PyPI at check date

claims.claim: Documented CLI flags: --data (required), --out (required), --dry-run, --base (default convaiinnovations/laya; accepts directory, built-in english/multilingual/typed-decisions, or Hub id), --loss rlcd|soft-ce, --shuffle-options, --label-smoothing 0.0, --freeze-encoder, --epochs 4, --micro-batch 8, --grad-accum 8, --encoder-lr 2.5e-5, --head-lr 1e-4, --max-len, --head-max-len, --eval/--eval-data, --target-error 0.10, --min-abstain-n 10, --device auto|CUDA|MPS|CPU, --seed 0; CSV also needs --text-column, --label-column, optional --question-id (default label) and --instructions.
claims.limits: There is no --model flag in the table; the base is --base. Some TrainConfig fields (amp, gradient_checkpointing, calib_max=400, calib_frac=0.1, option_layout) are not CLI flags.
claims.checks_gpt: CHAT: --data, --eval, --base multilingual, --device mps, --micro-batch, --grad-accum, --dry-run, --out. R2: laya-train --model convaiinnovations/laya

claims.claim: Data formats: CSV with one row per decision (text column + label column; label becomes a choice question over distinct values in first-appearance order); JSONL with per-line state, questions (type choice/noul/score, instructions, criteria for choice), expected (one answer per question), and optional gold teacher probabilities. Files may mix label shapes.
claims.values: noul expected true/false; score expected a level, fractional level splits weight (1.5 splits between levels 1 and 2)

claims.claim: Calibration and held-out: before training up to 400 items or 10% (whichever is smaller) is held out at a fixed seed; after the last epoch rank 0 fits one temperature per question type by LBFGS on log-temperature, clamped to [0.1, 10]; slice under ten items keeps 1.0; fit failure falls back to 1.2; temperatures written to rl_agent_config.json. Without --eval the 'after' numbers come from the calibration slice (report fields eval_mode, is_held_out, note say which).
claims.limits: The README separately says at checkpoint load temperatures are clamped to [0.5, 5.0] (C-C-06).

claims.claim: Hardware named by the Laya page: notebook uses two Kaggle T4 GPUs (internet on); benchmarks in issue #887 used one T4 per run; the browser-agent example uses a single 16 GB GPU; mixed precision on for CUDA, set amp=False on GTX 16xx. Update budget formula: epochs * ceil(ceil(train_items/micro_batch)/grad_accum); with defaults and 5,600 post-calibration items gives 352 updates.
claims.limits: The page names no Apple Silicon timing; the README names a separate Apple Silicon (MPS/CPU) notebook (C-02).

claims.claim: Laya README Calibration section: both checkpoints are over-confident as shipped; refitting one temperature per (question type, option count) on held-out data moves mean ECE 0.466 -> 0.081 for laya (English) and 0.314 -> 0.106 for laya-multilingual; laya-multilingual ships with no fitted temperatures. At load, numeric temperatures are clamped to [0.5, 5.0]; invalid entries use 1.0.
claims.quote: laya-multilingual ships with no fitted temperatures at all, so fit them before relying on its probabilities.
claims.limits: Condition: mean ECE over held-out data, per-(type, option-count) temperature fit. Benchmark name/sample size for this specific pair not stated in the lines read. The 0.466->0.081 pair is for the English 'laya' checkpoint, not multilingual.
claims.checks_gpt: CHAT: ECE 0.314->0.106 multilingual; compare with OrcaRouter 0.466->0.081

claims.claim: Related README ECE numbers: typed-decisions table (400 cases, 2,000 decisions, four workflows) lists ECE 0.213 for laya-typed-decisions, 0.174 for laya, 0.314 for laya-multilingual, 0.144 for published Jev 1.13.0; accuracy 0.766 / 0.362 / 0.352 / 0.727; random 0.318; majority class 0.461; teacher self-agreement ceiling 0.735.
claims.locator: README, 'typed-decisions, measured on all three checkpoints' table
claims.limits: The raw ECE 0.314 for laya-multilingual in this table is the same figure as the 'before' value in the Calibration section; the table is on typed-decisions zero-shot where base checkpoints are near chance. 0.766 comes from the checkpoint fine-tuned on that benchmark's own training split (README 'Honest limits').

claims.claim: pip install "laya[serve]" exists (adds fastapi + uvicorn + python-multipart); laya-serve binds 0.0.0.0:8000 in the README example, with env vars LAYA_DEVICE, LAYA_PRELOAD, LAYA_MODELS, LAYA_THREADS, LAYA_AUTO_TASK, LAYA_DEFAULT_MODEL, LAYA_MAX_LOADED, LAYA_IDLE_UNLOAD_SECONDS, LAYA_EXTRA_MODELS (JSON object name -> path/Hub id/[repo, subfolder]), LAYA_API_KEY (bearer). A client's model field is honoured when it names a Laya checkpoint (english/multilingual/typed-decisions, a LAYA_EXTRA_MODELS name, or a published Hub id); paths or unpublished Hub ids give 422; jev-1 and convaiinnovations/laya mean auto-route. Endpoints include /v1/systemone and /v1/systemone/batch.
claims.locator: README, serve section (lines ~746-795); JS client section (~455-480)
claims.values: port 8000 (example); 127.0.0.1 with LAYA_HOST in the JS-client example
claims.limits: Note: docs/finetune.md itself does not cover laya-serve or LAYA_EXTRA_MODELS (C-01); they are in the README.
claims.checks_gpt: CHAT: laya-serve with LAYA_EXTRA_MODELS and per-request model field, pip install "laya[serve]"

claims.claim: Laya inference via laya.load(path) (also Hub id), agent.predict(text, questions)["answers"]; finetune() from laya.train returns a report with train_items, calibration_items, skipped, epoch_loss, temperature, temperature_by_options, calibration.

claims.locator: pyproject [project.scripts]; npm registry for 'laya' (description 'build phaser project with template, data bind, and webpack hmr', latest 1.1.2)

claims.claim: Laya latency (Tesla T4): one question 39.5 ms (laya) and 32.8 ms (laya-multilingual); ten questions batched 158.6 ms and 72.3 ms; Apple MPS 4-question call 146 ms and 121 ms. Models: laya = ModernBERT-large 421M, English; laya-multilingual = mmBERT-base 322M, 100+ languages, up to 8,192 tokens.

claims.claim: Kev training command and flags: uv run python -m kev.train --data train.jsonl --base Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B-Base --init_from jaredpalmer/kev-4b --epochs 2 --lr 2e-5 --batch 1 --accum 8 --dtype bf16 --checkpointing 1 --device cuda --out runs/mine; also --full_ft 1, --p_none_pair, --suite, --base_revision, --n_per_source; --device auto tries CUDA then MPS then CPU; kev.train --help lists all options.
claims.checks_gpt: CHAT: uv run python -m kev.train flags (--data, --base, --init_from, --epochs, --lr...)

claims.claim: Kev JSONL training format: same shape as an API request plus a label on every question (choice = option name, noul = true/false, score = zero-based level position); keep 10-20% aside for evaluation. --init_from loads released adapter and pointer head; the trainer checks base, revision, LoRA rank and head size match.

Kev serving: uv run --extra serve python -m kev.serve --run jaredpalmer/kev-4b --port 8009; POST /v1/systemone on 8009; also GET /v1/models, POST /v1/systemone/permute and /v1/systemone/separate; binds 127.0.0.1 by default (--host 0.0.0.0 for other machines); KEV_API_KEY requires bearer token.
claims.locator: README serve section and API table

claims.claim: Kev Modal deploy: curl the skills/kev-deploy/scripts/kev_serve.py file, then KEV_API_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 24) modal deploy kev_serve.py; serves Kev-4B on an L40S at https://<workspace>--kev-api.modal.run; scales to zero, first request after idle waits about 35 s; KEV_MODEL selects another model; KEV_FLASH=1 KEV_REGION=us-east lowers warm latency but keeps one paid container; kev-deploy table gives $/h while up: Kev-0.8B L4 0.80, Kev-4B L40S 1.95, Kev-9B H100 3.95, Kev-27B B200 6.25.
claims.locator: README 'Deploy Your Own Endpoint'; kev-deploy SKILL.md section 2
claims.values: prices in USD/hour as listed by the skill
claims.limits: Prices are the skill's own table, not checked against Modal's price list.
claims.checks_gpt: CHAT: Modal deploy skill, KEV_API_KEY, KEV_MODEL

claims.claim: The default fine-tune route (kev-finetune skill) runs on Modal cloud GPUs and requires no local GPU: scripts convert/split data, then 'modal run scripts/kev_modal.py::train --data data/x --name x-v1 --init-from jaredpalmer/kev-4b', then deploy and teardown. The local path is 'By Hand' with kev.train on CUDA/MPS/CPU; --batch 1 --accum 8 in bf16 fits Kev-0.8B on a 4 GB GPU; on a Mac run one training job at a time; the 0.8B Mac path 'works but is slow for Qwen3.5 bases'.
claims.locator: kev-finetune README steps 1-7; Kev README 'By Hand'
claims.limits: Optional data generation calls an OpenAI-compatible API (~$0.25 per 1000 records with gpt-4.1-mini per the skill README), so data would leave the machine in that path.
claims.checks_gpt: Brief: note whether default fine-tune skill uses Modal

claims.claim: LoRA vs full fine-tune: Kev-0.8B, 4B, 9B use a rank-16 LoRA adapter plus pointer head on a frozen base (two epochs, cross-entropy, lr 1e-4 for 0.8B, 5e-5 for 4B and 9B); Kev-27B trains every backbone weight (--full_ft 1, lr 2e-6, one epoch on eight H200s, 145,840-record corpus), ships ~51 GB bf16 weights and needs an 80 GB GPU for serving.
claims.locator: README model table and training sections

claims.claim: Kev temperature calibration: each checkpoint stores a fitted temperature applied at load (Kev-0.8B 2.35, Kev-4B 2.41, Kev-9B 2.19, Kev-27B 1.32); on new sources Kev-9B calibration error fell 0.103 -> 0.041 and confident errors (>=0.9 probability) 8.2% -> 2.4% (README gives Jev's figure as 3.7%); KEV_TEMPERATURE=1.0 returns raw probabilities; scripts/calibrate_checkpoint.py provides an out-of-fold check. The fine-tune skill fits the temperature on a held-out slice of the user's data.
claims.locator: README Temperature / calibration section (WebFetch summary), kev-finetune README
claims.limits: Metric name behind 'calibration error' and suite size not captured beyond 'new sources' (transfer-v4, 764 records per README benchmark table).

claims.claim: Kev self-reported fine-tune result: one epoch on 5,219 labelled consumer-finance complaints raised Kev-4B accuracy from 0.804 to 0.904 on complaints it had never seen; README says such gains are in distribution.
claims.quote: one epoch on 5,219 labelled consumer-finance complaints took Kev-4B from 0.804 to 0.904 accuracy
claims.values: accuracy 0.804 -> 0.904; n_train 5,219; unseen-test size not stated in the line read
claims.limits: The README text says 'consumer-finance complaints' and does not name CFPB in the line read (keyword grep for 'CFPB' returned no match); GPT's 'CFPB' label is an inference. Test-set size not captured.
claims.checks_gpt: CHAT: 5,219 CFPB consumer complaints, Kev-4B accuracy 0.804->0.904

claims.claim: Kev example support workload: three questions, 1,050 generated records, 15 minutes on an H100; Kev-4B accuracy 67.7% -> 73.6% (95% CI on gain +2.3 to +9.7 points), Brier 0.402 -> 0.330; automation at a 5% error budget 34% -> 48%; with 400 records the gain was within noise; 'no change on the public evaluation data'.
claims.locator: kev-finetune README 'Why fine-tune at all'; Kev README
claims.limits: Generated (synthetic) records; one example workload.

claims.claim: Kev cost and latency: README and skill README say a Kev-4B training run costs about $1 on an H100; Kev-4B model time 18.1 ms for six questions on short text on an H100, 41.5 ms on an L40S (README speed claim); Apple M5 (32 GB) 721 ms for five questions on new text, 136 ms cached; ~101 requests/s in-process on H100. README also states the A100 is slower than the L40S for these models and costs more.
claims.locator: README Speed / hardware sections; kev-finetune README 'What you need'
claims.values: $1 per Kev-4B training run on H100; 18.1 ms on H100
claims.limits: The 18.1 ms figure is H100 model time (the latency_ms the API returns), not A100 and not end-to-end HTTP. Modal HTTP p50 for Kev-4B on one H100 at one client: 36.9 ms (direct server) vs 102.1 ms (regular web endpoint).
claims.checks_gpt: R2: Kev-4B training ~$1; 18 ms on A100

claims.claim: Kev hardware named by source: CUDA L4 (Kev-0.8B), L40S, H100, H200, B200; Kev-9B needs about 17 GB GPU memory; Kev-27B 51 GB weights (~66 GB with batching buffers); Apple Silicon via MLX measured on M5 32 GB; Kev-27B on 96-128 GB Mac is expected, not measured.
claims.locator: README model table and hardware notes

claims.claim: Simple Jev hf-server: Python 3.12+ install via pip install -e './hf-server'; start with python hf-server/hf_server.py --model Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B --device cpu --dtype float32 ...; listens on 127.0.0.1:8000; POST /v1/classifier is the main endpoint and /v1/systemone is an alias of it; GET /v1/models, /health, /docs; also --backend laya with --model convaiinnovations/laya --subfolder typed-decisions. Public demo API at simple-jev-demo-api.featherless.ai has a 2k-token context limit and 2 requests per second.
claims.locator: README 'Running the HF Server', 'How do I use the API?', 'Try it today'
claims.values: demo: 2k tokens, 2 RPS (README); a search snippet cites 4 requests/s on a playground page, not verified
claims.limits: The server scores answer-token logits and does not generate JSON text. The README says the GPU example is 'a launch example, not a verified full-size Gemma benchmark'.

claims.claim: RFDT (Really Fancy Decision Training) is in the Simple Jev repo today: prepare.py (validate, teacher-label missing targets via an OpenAI-compatible chat API, whole-group splits), train.py (selected-label cross-entropy on allowed answer-token logits, LoRA via --lora, torchrun multi-GPU), export.py (merge LoRA for the HF server). Example multi-GPU command uses four BF16 NVIDIA GPUs, --lora --lora-rank 16, batch 2 x accum 8, 3 epochs, lr 1e-4; a CPU smoke run with --cpu --max-steps 2 is documented. Scripts are 'not a GPU provisioning service'. Hosted fine-tuned model support and fine-tuning on Featherless are described as an upcoming rollout, not available.
claims.quote: The scripts are an initial training workflow, not a GPU provisioning service.
claims.locator: RFDT/README.md; main README section 'One more thing: RFDT'
claims.limits: Teacher-authored probabilities are recorded as teacher_authored_probabilities, not measured token distributions. The cache and prepared files contain the user's context and teacher answers; the teacher call sends contexts to the configured endpoint.

claims.claim: JevAny training and serving: 'jevany train --config recipes/sft.toml' (starter: Qwen3.5-0.8B on CUDA, BF16, output runs/my-jev), 'recipes/finetune.toml' to adapt the released 27B on own JSONL (--data), experimental RLCR recipe (recipes/rlcr.toml) rewarding correctness and calibration; GPU guidance ~8 GB BF16 weights for 4B and ~54 GB for 27B plus runtime memory; serve with 'jevany serve --checkpoint <id> --device cuda --dtype bf16 --port 8008'; JevClient.system_one(state, questions); README reports up to 3.72x median latency reduction on H200 for the 27B model. Apache-2.0. README mentions neither RFDT, hf-server nor /v1/classifier.
claims.limits: Read only through a fetch summary; no GitHub API check, so commit/creation dates unknown and README wording not re-read line by line.

claims.claim: WeChat article could not be read; claimed figures (Laya multilingual zero-shot 18.45% on Chinese game intent classification; bert-base-chinese fine-tuned to 95%+; 33 ms) are unverified.
claims.limits: Blocked by verification page. Laya's own README (C-02) states base checkpoints are near chance zero-shot on typed-decisions (0.362 and 0.352 vs random 0.318) and says 'Laya is a fast base to specialise'; this is a different task and not the WeChat test. The CHAT's remark that zero-shot Laya and fine-tuned bert-base-chinese are not a same-model before/after is consistent with the claim as described.

claims.claim: Hamel/Saha procedure for threshold calibration: models return failure probability per trace; dataset of 100 apartment-leasing agent traces (98 scored; frozen reference 61 failures and 37 without a labeled failure); labels binary (1 = failure). Threshold selection: maximize F1 while requiring at least 80% precision and 80% recall, via stratified five-fold cross-validation (choose thresholds on training split, measure on held-out, same splits for every model, results averaged over repeated splits); if no threshold meets both minimums use the unconstrained F1 optimum and record the split as infeasible. Infeasible in 36 of 100 training splits for Perplexity, 29 for Liquid d1-ultra, never for OpenAI.
claims.quote: tune a decision threshold to maximize F1 while requiring at least 80% precision and 80% recall
claims.locator: section on tuning the decision threshold; coding-agent prompt boxes
claims.values: default threshold 0.50; 5-fold stratified CV; 100 training splits implied
claims.limits: Single dataset of 98 traces; the authors say minimums guide selection but do not guarantee performance on new data. Threshold tuning was run by a coding agent on saved scores, with no new model calls.
claims.checks_gpt: CHAT: Hamel Husain and Antaripa Saha, 2026-10-20, threshold calibration with cross-validation

claims.claim: Hamel/Saha probability calibration check: Platt scaling fit on log-odds after clipping probabilities away from 0 and 1, stratified five-fold CV with the same splits across models, reliability plot with five groups of ~19-20 traces. Brier before -> after: Jev 0.187 -> 0.188; Liquid d1-ultra 0.173 -> 0.172; OpenAI 0.159 -> 0.164 (exploratory direct refit 0.154). Calibration helped Perplexity, Liquid d1 and Clef Flash (one Clef Flash group averaged ~8% predicted failure with ~60% actual); Jev and Liquid d1-ultra were already well calibrated on this dataset.
claims.limits: Out-of-fold probability summaries on 98 traces; Brier mixes calibration and discrimination (also stated by scikit-learn docs C-22). The post does not report ECE.

claims.claim: Hamel/Saha model set and cost/F1: Jev 1.13, Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Cloudflare Clef Flash, OpenAI Decisions (GPT-6 Luna); OpenAI highest F1 0.87 at 3.72 cents per 100 eval runs; Perplexity cheapest at 0.82 cents per 100 runs with F1 0.79 (about 4.5x cost ratio). All models accessed by vendor APIs; no hardware reported. Mean response times 4.33 s (Jev), 7.85 s, 7.38 s, 1.56 s, 2.09 s, 2.77 s from separate runs, not treated as comparative latency.
claims.limits: Vendor API prices at time of writing (Liquid prices as of 2026-10-17).

claims.claim: Transformers text-classification guide: fine-tunes DistilBERT on IMDb with AutoModelForSequenceClassification (num_labels, id2label, label2id), DataCollatorWithPadding, TrainingArguments (learning_rate 2e-5, per_device batch 16, 2 epochs, weight_decay 0.01, eval_strategy epoch, load_best_model_at_end), accuracy via evaluate; inference with pipeline('sentiment-analysis') or logits argmax. The guide reports no hardware.
claims.limits: Binary example; no calibration or probability thresholding covered.

claims.claim: PEFT LoRA guide: freezes base weights and trains low-rank update matrices; LoraConfig parameters r, target_modules, lora_alpha, bias, use_rslora, modules_to_save (for a randomly initialized task head), layers_to_transform, rank_pattern, alpha_pattern; merge_and_unload() merges the adapter so there is no added inference latency; loftq initialization for quantized models; no hardware named, only qualitative memory claims.
claims.limits: lora_dropout not listed on this page.

claims.claim: QLoRA abstract: finetune a 65B-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance; introduces 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), double quantization, paged optimizers; Guanaco reaches 99.3% of ChatGPT on the Vicuna benchmark after 24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU; over 1,000 models finetuned across 8 instruction datasets.
claims.limits: Instruction-tuning of generative LLMs, not classification heads.

claims.claim: SetFit docs: prompt-free few-shot fine-tuning of Sentence Transformers; with 8 labeled examples per class on Customer Reviews it is competitive with RoBERTa Large fine-tuned on the full 3k training set; typically an order of magnitude or more faster to train and infer; works with any Sentence Transformer including multilingual checkpoints.
claims.limits: Index page only; license, API and hardware not on this page.

claims.claim: ModernBERT-base card: Apache-2.0; ~149M parameters; 22 layers; context up to 8,192 tokens; trained on ~2 trillion tokens of English text and code (8x H100); primarily English, lower performance expected on other languages; recommends fine-tuning with standard BERT recipes for classification; needs transformers >= 4.48.0; Flash Attention 2 recommended on supported GPUs.

mmBERT-base card: MIT; 307M parameters (110M non-embedding); '1800+' languages (decay phase covers 1833); >3T training tokens; 8,192-token context; ModernBERT architecture with Gemma 2 tokenizer (256k vocab); example scripts for dense retrieval, XNLI cross-lingual classification (lr 3e-5, 3 epochs) and cross-encoder reranking (lr 2e-5, 2 epochs); claims to outperform XLM-R without numbers on the card.
claims.limits: Card has no limitations section or benchmark numbers.

claims.claim: bert-base-chinese card: Apache-2.0, Google, Fill-Mask, 12 layers, vocab 21,128, ~0.1B parameters; training data and evaluation results are '[More Information Needed]'. hfl/chinese-roberta-wwm-ext card: Apache-2.0, HIT/iFLYTEK Joint Laboratory, Chinese BERT with Whole Word Masking; card instructs to load with 'Bert' classes despite the RoBERTa name; training corpus not stated on the card; cites arXiv:2004.13922 and 1906.08101.
claims.quote: Please use 'Bert' related functions to load this model!
claims.limits: Second card is C-20; the single-source field here points to C-19.

claims.claim: Guo et al. 2017 abstract: temperature scaling, a single-parameter variant of Platt scaling, is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions on most datasets; scikit-learn guide documents temperature scaling as method='temperature': softmax(z/T) on logits, T learned by minimizing log loss on a calibration set, one parameter, argmax and accuracy unchanged. scikit-learn also documents CalibratedClassifierCV (cv, ensemble, FrozenEstimator for prefit models), sigmoid vs isotonic (isotonic roughly 1000+ samples), reliability diagrams via CalibrationDisplay/calibration_curve, and warns Brier score/log loss mix calibration with resolution.
claims.locator: scikit-learn 'Multiclass support'; CalibratedClassifierCV; calibration curves (C-21 for the paper)
claims.limits: ECE is not defined in either read page; calibrator should be fit on data independent of the classifier's training data (scikit-learn).

claims.claim: Geifman and El-Yaniv 2017 abstract: builds a selective classifier (reject option) from an already-trained network; the user sets a desired risk level and the classifier rejects inputs as needed to meet it with high probability; on ImageNet a top-5 error of 2% is guaranteed with 99.9% probability at almost 60% test coverage.
claims.limits: Abstract only; risk-coverage details not read.

claims.claim: TEI serving: /predict is for sequence classification models (example SamLowe/roberta-base-go_emotions) and /rerank for re-rankers (example BAAI/bge-reranker-large) via docker run with --model-id; docs state TEI 'currently supports CamemBERT, and XLM-RoBERTa Sequence Classification models with absolute positions', while the example table also lists GTE, ModernBERT and RoBERTa classifiers; hardware: CPU, Turing, Ampere 80/86, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, Blackwell; CUDA compute capability below 7.5 (V100, GTX 1000) unsupported. TEI's own index describes it as a toolkit for text embeddings models.
claims.values: image tags *-1.9; port 8080 mapped in examples
claims.limits: The docs do not say whether a custom fine-tuned Chinese BERT classifier is supported; BERT is listed under embeddings, not under classification.

claims.claim: vLLM pooling docs: 'classify' task outputs a probability vector per sequence; models whose architecture name matches *For*Classification are converted with --convert classify; default LAST pooling, softmax; activation chosen from HF problem_type, then Sentence Transformers metadata, then sigmoid/softmax by label count; use_activation=false returns raw logits; /classify endpoint corresponds to LLM.classify; /score and /rerank endpoints exist for cross-encoders with num_labels equal to 1.
claims.limits: Separate Classification API request-format page not read.

claims.claim: ONNX serving references: Optimum ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_id, export=True) exports and loads a sequence classifier in ONNX; onnxruntime (CPU) and onnxruntime-gpu (CUDA 12.x default) are separate pip packages, only one per environment; Triton lists TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX, OpenVINO, Python among backends, offers dynamic batching and HTTP/REST and gRPC (KServe-based) endpoints, and the landing page says nothing about classifiers specifically.
claims.locator: Optimum models guide; ONNX Runtime get-started; Triton landing (C-27)
claims.limits: No latency or throughput claims in the pages read.

claims.claim: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024) Section 2.4 Data Privacy: GAI training requires large volumes of data that may include personal data, raising risks to transparency, individual participation (consent) and purpose specification; model developers mostly do not disclose training sources; models may leak or infer sensitive information, and memorization can cause risk even for data present in few training samples. Section 2.5 notes inference energy is higher for generative tasks than for discriminative tasks such as text classification.
claims.limits: Profile is voluntary guidance for generative AI; suggested actions in Section 3 were not read, so no action IDs are recorded.

claims.claim: OWASP LLM04:2025 Data and Model Poisoning: data used to pre-train, fine-tune or create embeddings can be tampered with; mitigations include tracking data provenance (ML-BOM, CycloneDX), dataset version control (DVC), vetting data vendors, sandboxing unverified data, access controls on training infrastructure, monitoring training loss, red-team testing. OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure: training or fine-tuning data can resurface in outputs; mitigations include data sanitization before training, federated learning, differential privacy, least-privilege access for training pipelines. LLM03:2025 Supply Chain covers malicious or vulnerable LoRA adapters and weak model provenance.
claims.limits: Read through fetch summaries; entries are LLM-oriented rather than classifier-specific.
